title: Why: The Most Important Question in Life
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: A traveler asked three stonecutters at a cathedral building site what they were doing. “Cutting stone,” the first one grumbled. “Earning a living,” said the second. The third looked up: “I’m building a cathedral.” The same work, the same tools, three different lives. One word set them apart: why.

A psychiatrist who survived the concentration camps recorded an observation that neither strength nor health could explain: those who had something to live for were more likely to survive. A face waiting for them, a child, unfinished work. Those who had their “why” could bear almost any “how”; those who lost it faded within a few weeks. Meaning isn’t a luxury; it’s oxygen. Research today confirms this far from the camps: people with a sense of meaning are healthier, more resilient, and live longer. And happiness can’t be chased down directly: pursued, it flies away; it settles on its own when you are doing something worthwhile. This is also where burnout comes from: seldom from too much work, more often from work cut off from meaning, because money motivates only up to a certain threshold, and beyond it the strength to get out of bed has to come from something else.

Where should you look for your “why”? Along three paths: in the work you give the world; in the people you love, because meaning surprisingly often has a name and a phone number; and in your stance toward suffering that can’t be avoided. It helps to turn the question around: not “What do I want from life?” but “What is life asking of me today?” In Japan, famous for its longevity, there is a special word for the reason you get up in the morning, and people there tend it as carefully as their diet. And here is a simple exercise: ask “why” of your work five times in a row, and somewhere around the fourth time you will uncover what truly carries your days. Then reframe one duty: not “I’m cooking dinner” but “I’m feeding my family.” The Teacher of Ecclesiastes, a man who succeeded at everything, summed up life without a “why” in a few words: futile, a chasing after the wind.

We ask “What am I living for?” only because we suspect an answer exists. The Bible confirms that suspicion: you are not an accident, you were created on purpose, and cathedrals are built at the kitchen sink and the office desk too.

questions: What do you get up in the morning for, and would your answer carry you through a really hard Monday?
Which of your duties looks like cutting stone but is really building a cathedral?

paragraphs: An old story tells of a traveler who, at the building site of a medieval cathedral, asked three stonecutters what they were doing. The first grumbled, “Cutting stone.” The second said, “Earning a living for my family.” The third set down his chisel, looked up, and answered, “I’m building a cathedral.” All three were doing exactly the same work, with the same tools, for the same pay. And yet they lived in three different worlds. One invisible word set them apart: why.

How great a difference that makes was most powerfully attested by a Viennese psychiatrist who survived the concentration camps and lost nearly all his loved ones there. He observed something there that neither physical strength nor health could explain: amid extreme hunger and violence, those more likely to survive were not the strongest, but those who had something to live for. A wife’s face waiting for them. A child. An unfinished book that had to be reconstructed from memory. Those who had their “why” could bear almost any “how.” Those who lost it faded within a few weeks, even though objectively nothing new was happening to them. From these observations grew one of the most important insights of twentieth-century psychology: meaning is not a luxury of a successful life. It is oxygen.

Modern research confirms this in settings far removed from the camps. People with a strong sense of meaning are healthier, more resilient to stress and depression, and even live longer, regardless of how well-off they are. Interestingly, meaning and pleasure are two different things, and confusing them costs a great deal. Happiness can’t be chased down directly: pursued, it flies away like a butterfly, but it settles on its own when a person is busy with something they consider worthwhile. That’s why, on an evening of “I’m not happy,” a new pleasure rarely helps, while one meaningful thing done for someone surprisingly often does.

Here, too, lies the key to a phenomenon our times know all too well: burnout. Despite the name, burnout doesn’t come from too much work alone. People can work hard for years without burning out if they see why. What burns people out is work cut off from meaning: reports nobody reads, effort nobody notices, tasks that change nothing in anyone’s life. Financial motivation works in a similar way: money motivates strongly, but only up to a certain threshold, beyond which a raise brings joy about as briefly as a new phone, and the daily strength to get out of bed has to come from something else. Companies that have understood this have stopped telling people only “what” and “how much” and have started showing them whom their work serves. Anyone who has watched people just after retirement knows a similar lesson: some flourish, others visibly fade within a year, and the difference seldom lies in health or money. It lies in whether a person lost their “why” along with their job, or managed to transfer it: to grandchildren, to service, to a garden, to a community. In Japan, famous for its longevity, there is a special word for this, meaning the reason you get up in the morning, and older people there tend that reason as carefully as their diet.

The business world discovered the same truth by looking at the companies and leaders people really follow. You can draw it as three circles. The outer one is “what”: products, tasks, duties; anyone can list them. The middle one is “how”: methods and approaches. And at the very center sits “why”: the reason all of it exists. Most people and organizations communicate from the outside in: we do this and that, buy, do, get it done. Those who inspire others start from the inside: we believe this and that, and that’s why we do what we do. People don’t follow what you do but why you do it, because “why” reaches the place where decisions are made: emotions, trust, and belonging. This works in a company, but it works just the same in a family and inside your own head: a duty propped up only by “what” cracks on the first hard Monday; a duty propped up by “why” holds for years. A well-known anecdote tells of a president touring a space center who asked a man with a mop what he did there. “Mr. President, I’m helping put a man on the moon,” he replied. You can smile at that, but the man was telling the truth: without spotless rooms, the delicate spaceflight technology wouldn’t stand a chance. He simply saw the whole picture in which his mop had a place.

Where should you look for your own “why”? The same psychiatrist who survived the camps pointed to three paths, and none of them requires extraordinary circumstances. The first is work: something you give the world, a job, service, something done well. The second is love: the people you love and who need you, because meaning surprisingly often has a name and a phone number. The third, and the hardest, is attitude: in the face of suffering that can’t be avoided, there remains the choice of how to carry it, and that choice is meaning too. You can see this in people who, after a serious diagnosis, start support groups for other patients, or who, after losing a child, help parents going through the same darkness. They don’t claim the suffering was good. They claim it doesn’t have to be barren, and that difference changes everything: the same burden, carried with meaning and without it, becomes two different burdens. He also advised turning our usual question around. Instead of “What do I want from life?” ask, “What is life asking of me today?” The answer can be disarmingly concrete: someone is waiting for a conversation with you, some matter is waiting for your honesty, someone needs you simply to show up.

It’s also worth knowing what a life that avoids this question looks like, and here the Bible has a text that predates all modern diagnoses by three thousand years. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes, a man who succeeded at everything, conducted a total experiment on himself: he amassed wealth, fame, pleasures, great buildings, and denied himself nothing. And then he summed it up: futility of futilities, everything is futile, a chasing after the wind. This isn’t the voice of a failure but of a winner who reached the summit and found that the summit itself explains nothing. The Teacher’s diagnosis sounds surprisingly fresh today, because it describes a civilization that has more and more “what” and less and less “why.”

Here’s a practice for this week. Take your everyday work and ask it “why” five times in a row, going deeper each time: I clean the house. Why? So it’s clean. Why? So the people I live with feel good at home. Why? Usually somewhere around the fourth “why,” something is uncovered that truly carries your days. Then try writing down one sentence: what I get up in the morning for. It doesn’t have to be lofty; it has to be yours. And reframe one duty the way the third stonecutter did: not “I’m cooking dinner” but “I’m feeding my family”; not “I’m doing spreadsheets” but “I’m making sure people get paid on time.” This isn’t playing with words. It’s reclaiming the cathedral that has been standing over your chisel all along. And at the end of the week, do a short review with one question: at what moments did I feel that what I was doing had meaning? Your answers, gathered week after week, will form a map of your “why” more reliably than any musing at a desk, because meaning leaves its tracks in days actually lived, not in theories.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Three stonecutters do the same work but live in three different worlds, because their “why” sets them apart. A psychiatrist who survived the camps recorded that those who had something to live for were the ones who survived: meaning is not a luxury but oxygen, and research today links it to health, resilience, and longevity. Meaning is different from pleasure: happiness pursued flies away, but settles on its own when you are doing work worth doing. Look for your own “why” along three paths: in the work you give, in the people you love, and in your stance toward what you can’t change, asking not “What do I want from life?” but “What is life asking of me today?” It helps to ask “why” of your own work five times, to write down one sentence about what you get up for, and to reframe a duty from “cutting stone” to “building a cathedral.”

sections.heading: Look Higher
paragraphs: The very question “What am I living for?” reveals something important: we ask about purpose only when we suspect an answer exists. We ask what a hammer is for, because someone made it for something. The Bible answers that suspicion directly: you are not an accident or a by-product; you were created on purpose, and God prepared in advance the good works that are to be your way of life. This changes the status of every piece of honest work: calling stops being a privilege of the clergy and becomes an ordinary day lived before God. Cathedrals are built at the kitchen sink too, at the office desk, and at the bedside of an ailing parent. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes, after his great experiment, arrived at the same threshold: everything is fleeting until it finds its footing in the One who does not pass away. For the deepest “why” is not something a person invents. It is something they discover, the way you discover the author’s design in a well-written book. Jesus Himself said that He knew where He came from and where He was going, and that certainty carried Him through nights that would have broken anyone. Whoever knows their “where from” and “where to” will not have the ground cut out from under their feet by any “how.”
